news.title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
news.title_en: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.

“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.

Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.

Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.

The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.

Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.

OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.

As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.

Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.

“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
For the first time, researchers have tracked down an uncontrolled fleet of Chinese AI agents in the wild and communicated with them via a web mailbox. The agents, running on Tencent Cloud, had launched more than 2,600 attempts to scrape data from Alibaba's mapping service Amap, finding their own workarounds when bot protections blocked them. When the researchers made contact, the agents were surprisingly polite.

news.title: CoreWeave stock drops 15%+ and its bond yields near 15%, over concerns that some tech companies are borrowing too heavily for the AI build-out; ORCL drops 8%+ (Michelle Fox/CNBC)
news.title_en: CoreWeave stock drops 15%+ and its bond yields near 15%, over concerns that some tech companies are borrowing too heavily for the AI build-out; ORCL drops 8%+ (Michelle Fox/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
CoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out.

Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 16%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.

Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said.

"The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back."

Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090, called out CoreWeave's soaring yields on X late Tuesday. That prompted Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to respond, "yikes."

Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of his deep dive into whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk."

CoreWeave's balance sheet is "relatively bad" compared to its neocloud peers, said Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. That's because CoreWeave has done more borrowing and is currently building more data centers, he explained.

"The yields have blown out because there's just more and more concern — that I don't share — about the wherewithal of these guys [being] able to over time pay back their interest expense," Meeks said.

"It's definitely not a deteriorating situation," he added. "Maybe it's not improving, and I didn't really expect it to improve until these data centers get up and running."

CoreWeave, 1 monthHe expects the company to report flat margins from June to September and guide for margins to have a pretty significant improvement between September and December. CoreWeave's next quarterly results are expected in November.

CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. For instance, shares of Oracle tumbled nearly 7% on Wednesday. Yields on its bonds were also higher, with the yield to maturity on its 6.25% bond due in Nov. 2032 sitting at 7.24%.

The overall tech sector brought down the stock market on Wednesday with the Nasdaq Composite losing 1.4%. The debt concern seems to be hitting the shakier stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven" the hardest.

Another neocloud stock, Nebius, dropped 9%. Dell cratered by 10%.

Companies are in a race to build AI infrastructure and have turned to the credit market to finance their projects, leading to a jump in supply.

Overall, hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion this year, according to JPMorgan. By 2027, it is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually, the bank said.

ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI has filed legal allegations that a former employee stole over 100 confidential documents—including unreleased device specs and supply chain data—and presented them to Apple leadership before joining the company.

news.title: WhatsApp rolls out a guest calling feature letting people join a call even if they don't have an account; guests cannot start a call and have to be invited (Anna Washenko/Engadget)
news.title_en: WhatsApp rolls out a guest calling feature letting people join a call even if they don't have an account; guests cannot start a call and have to be invited (Anna Washenko/Engadget)
news.author: Engadget
news.article_content:
WhatsApp
                    
                        
            
                Add Engadget on Google:
                
                    Preferred Source
                    Google Discover
                
            
        
				            
                
                
                WhatsApp is adding more flexibility for talking to people who aren't regular users of its service. The Meta-owned company has announced the addition of a feature dubbed guest calling. With this option, somebody can join a call even if they don't have a WhatsApp account.

The guest calling support mirrors the little-known option to join a FaceTime call without an Apple account or device. Like that feature, there are some restrictions for participating in a WhatsApp call via the guest method. Guests cannot start a call; they can only receive and accept invitations. They'll also have to be approved by the call host before they can join. A guest will not be able to view other users' phone numbers, send messages or add more members to the call. However, they will be able to join either 1:1 or group calls from a browser, and once approved, guests will be able to use core tools such as screen sharing, raising their hand, and reacting with the thumbs up and heart emojis. Guests also won't have any time limits placed on their participation in a call.

The company noted that it plans to further facilitate collaboration with the future rollout of a plugin for calendar integrations. Once launched "later this year," the plugin will allow WhatApp calls can be created from Google or Outlook calendars.

WhatsApp has kept a brisk pace with feature updates this year, many of them aimed at making the service more accessible, secure and appealing for business users. The addition of usernames allowed people to keep their phone numbers private, while more incremental adds from 2026 include encrypted web calls and account signups via iPad. The service may also offer a much-requested option to schedule messages in advance.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 这是WhatsApp终于想通了：想从微信和Zoom嘴里抢人，就得先别逼人注册。把门槛降低到点链接就能进，不过是想在还没把用户彻底绑架前，先让他们习惯“没我不行”。

news.title: OpenAI will reportedly ship at least one model this year but its flagship still needs alignment work
news.title_en: OpenAI will reportedly ship at least one model this year but its flagship still needs alignment work
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
OpenAI is racing to finish its next flagship model, which uses the same looped transformer technique as Astra to boost math and coding performance. The tradeoff is that looping makes safety monitoring harder. Microsoft accidentally revealed details about how the technique works on a public page. Whether or not the flagship is ready in time, employees say one or two new models will likely ship by year's end.

news.title: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
news.title_en: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning.

Researchers with the company say they've found a new, cost-effective way to make more accurate weather forecasts two to six weeks in advance - allowing farmers and emergency responders to plan ahead with greater certainty. The findings were published today in the journal Nature, and the tool is now open-source software.

news.article_content:
Square is launching new hardware: a big kiosk for ordering things that has a touchscreen and lets you talk to an AI. It's called the Square Kiosk.

news.title: Salience Labs, which develops specialized all-optical circuit switching tech for AI data centers, raised a $125M Series B led by Bullhound Capital (Mike Wheatley/SiliconANGLE)
news.title_en: Salience Labs, which develops specialized all-optical circuit switching tech for AI data centers, raised a $125M Series B led by Bullhound Capital (Mike Wheatley/SiliconANGLE)
news.author: SiliconANGLE
news.article_content:
SHARE


	
	
		
			
				
					
						UPDATED 09:00 EDT / OCTOBER 14 2026

A startup called Salience Labs Inc. wants to play a bigger role in speeding up artificial intelligence workloads after raising $125 million in a Series B funding.

Today’s round was led by Bullhound Capital and saw the two of the chipmaking industry’s most iconic names participate via their investment arms, Intel Capital AMD Ventures. SBI Group, Hudson River Trading and the British Business Bank were also named as new investors, while existing backers including Applied Ventures, Oxford Science Enterprises, Cambridge Innovation Capital and Silicon Catalyst Ventures returned to get involved again.

Salience Labs is the developer of specialized all-optical circuit switching technology for AI data centers, and it has attracted a lot of interest thanks to the unprecedented strain being placed on existing infrastructure. As co-founder and Chief Executive Vaysh Kewada explains, most data centers today still rely on traditional networking fabrics based on electronic switches and repeated optical-to-electrical-to-optical signal conversions to keep traffic flowing efficiently.

But Kewada says the problem is that they’re not, in fact, that efficient, because these legacy fabrics simply cannot keep up with the massive throughput demands of AI computing clusters made up of tens of thousands of graphics processing units and other accelerators. The available interconnect bandwidth is seriously lagging behind that of the raw compute capacity now available, resulting in latency bottlenecks and growing power consumption that dramatically drives up the cost of AI workloads.

Kewada is convinced that the best way to get rid of these networking chokepoints is to eliminate electrical signals in the data center completely, and that means making sure data is only transmitted over optical connections. To do this, Salience Labs has developed an all-optical and fully integrated silicon photonics-based network switch architecture.

It’s targeted at high-density workloads, and instead of feeding massive data packets into GPUs electrically, it dynamically routes information directly on-chip, ensuring that it arrives at its destination much more rapidly. This results in much lower latency and significantly reduced power consumption, paving the way for companies to scale their GPU clusters to hundreds of thousands of chips.

“Optical circuit switching will play a critical role in AI data center networking,” Kewada said. “As customers roll out optical links in their data centers, high-performance optical switches are needed to deliver the token economics that AI workloads demand.”

Salience Labs recently demonstrated the most advanced version of its optical circuit-switching tech at the ECOC 2026 conference in September, showcasing the world’s first 64-port all-optical photonic switch. The company said the switch not only validates its approach to optical switching, but also lays the groundwork for even more rapid communications, with denser 128-port and 256-port configurations now under development.

These devices will support the “scale-up and scale-out” of network fabrics across data-intensive environments, Kewada promised. It’s targeting a massive opportunity too, with data from Cignal AI forecasting the market for optical circuit switching to grow to more than $8 billion by the end of the decade. Today’s funding round will help to ensure it grabs a piece of this pie, with the money set to be directed toward volume manufacturing and geographic market expansion, as well as the research and development of the company’s higher-density switches.

Intel Capital’s Srini Ananth said most data center operators already recognize that photonic switches are the future and will soon become omnipresent in all modern AI factories. “Optical switching can unlock significant gains in performance and efficiency,” he said. “Salience Labs stands out through its integrated silicon photonics architecture and proprietary optical amplification, addressing key challenges to deploying optical switching at scale.”

news.title: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: gorgeous screen, Android apps, and nice design and build quality, but Amazon's bloatware is pervasive and Alexa+ is subpar (David Pierce/The Verge)
news.title_en: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: gorgeous screen, Android apps, and nice design and build quality, but Amazon's bloatware is pervasive and Alexa+ is subpar (David Pierce/The Verge)
news.author: The Verge
news.article_content:

The screen is gorgeous, the hardware works, and it finally runs full Android. But there’s too much Amazon in my tablet.

We have to talk about this screen. It’s the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It’s a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls “Nanomatte” that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen.

The $549.99 device I’ve been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you don’t really need. The pitch for all those devices is the same: They’re well-made, midrange tablets that can access the full universe of Android apps through the Play Store and come with a whole bunch of Amazon bloatware whether you want it or not. I haven’t tested those other devices, but I’m glad they exist — cheap, good Android tablets are too hard to come by.

Amazon bloatware everywhereAlexa Plus isn’t greatSome middling specs

But the Nanomatte. The Nanomatte! The etching on the display, which Amazon says it partnered with Corning to do at a sub-pixel level to reduce glare without causing the slight rainbow-shimmering effect you can get on other matte screens, absolutely does its job. When I use my iPad outdoors, I can often see what’s behind me like I’m staring into a mirror; the 12 Pro reflects only a small sheen of light, and does it without losing any sharpness. The viewing angles are incredible, too. I’d like the display to be a little brighter, but since the main reason to crank the brightness is to fight glare, it hasn’t really been a problem.

The screen is not perfect. The anti-glare texture gives the Alexa Tablet a bit of shimmer, especially when you’re looking at light text on a black background. And the iPad’s blacks are still blacker; watching a movie, the letterboxes above and below are still slightly lit on the Alexa Tablet’s LCD, and they’re just flat-out off on the iPad’s OLED panel. Some of this you can fix: The 12 Pro has specific modes that automatically tweak tone and color to make reading more pleasant, and you can even control the overall picture through a few presets like the ones you’d find on your TV. My review unit came with “Boosted” mode turned on, which made every color just a smidge too colorful. I turned it to “Natural” and immediately liked the picture better.

I’m not sure this screen counts as some revolution in display technology, but then again, I did reflexively say “whoa” the first second I turned it on, and all that was showing was the Amazon logo. I like this display for everything. The 120Hz refresh rate looks great when running Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and the 3:2 aspect ratio feels right for web browsing and side-by-side work. The more muted display modes even make reading more pleasant than your average giant screen, though it’s lame that they only work in the Kindle app. After a few days of using the tablet indoors and out, I prefer the 12 Pro’s screen to any iPad I’ve tried. (Unfortunately, I don’t have an iPad Pro with the nano-texture glass to compare it to, but that’s a $2,200 tablet. I doubt anyone’s debating between the two.)

All that display tech in a $549.99 device requires tradeoffs basically everywhere else, and Amazon makes lots of them. The MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor benchmarks somewhere between a flagship high-end Android phone from last year and a flagship phone from two years ago, and gets absolutely lapped by practically every current iPad. In one graphics-heavy benchmark, the current 13-inch iPad Pro scored about nine times higher.

I’d like more horsepower here, but in my day-to-day use there’s plenty of power in this tablet. In several days of playing games, doing work, and watching a lot of NFL RedZone, the only slowness I’ve detected has been little niggling things in the Android experience. The app switcher sometimes stutters when it loads. I suppose I worry a little about how this tablet will age, given that it doesn’t share the iPad’s preposterous oversupply of processing power, but for now it’s fine.

Come to think of it, “it’s fine” explains most of the 12 Pro’s hardware. The four speakers are a little thin and muddy, but loud and clear enough. The cameras wash out some colors, but they work for video calls. The $149.99 keyboard case is nice to type on, but a little awkward to detach and manipulate. The $89.99 pen is smooth and responsive, but not many Android apps support a stylus. The battery lasts me about eight hours of screen time, which is a little less than I’d like and less than Amazon advertises. Nothing here is a deal-breaker, it’s just a lot of fine.

The software, on the other hand, is all extremes. The great news: The Alexa Tablets run full Android, not the weird off-brand operating system Amazon’s Fire tablets have used for the last 15 years. That means you get all the apps in the Play Store, a vastly improved interface, and access to things like Google’s Gemini assistant. All by itself, that change makes these the most functional Amazon tablets ever.

If you’re going to say you “obsess over customers,” you don’t get to borrow the top left corner of my homescreen and then use that space to show me an ad vaguely offering to “Cook with premium ingredients” that launches an also unhideable Alexa chat window in the bottom right corner of my homescreen.

Luckily, this is Android, and installing a new launcher takes 30 seconds. If you buy an Alexa Tablet, I recommend doing so immediately.

I would be less annoyed by Alexa’s overbearing presence on this tablet if Alexa Plus were actually useful, which it mostly is not. If you’re looking to buy whatever’s on your screen, Alexa’s your bot: You can invoke the assistant in any app, and it’ll almost always assume your goal is to shop for whatever you’re currently looking at. If you want, well, anything else, you’re probably out of luck. Almost a year after its launch, Alexa Plus is not a very good assistant. It’s slow, it gets lost in back-and-forth conversations, and it still doesn’t have enough access to my apps and data to be useful. You can switch to Gemini in the device’s settings, and you should.

Once you de-Amazon the tablet, you’re left with a pretty useful Android device. And this is where the Alexa Tablet gets tricky to evaluate. I wouldn’t recommend using it as a primary computer, given the still sorry state of large-screen Android apps. (Between this and the ongoing Googlebook fiasco, I really hope Google is learning a lesson about incentivizing developers to care about big screens and keyboards.) But between the Kindle-specific display mode, all the streaming and reading apps in the Play Store, and this terrific screen, this is immediately one of the best tablets-for-tablet-things you can buy.

Realistically, you’re probably debating whether to buy the Alexa Tablet or an iPad. (Apologies to the Samsung Galaxy Tab shoppers out there, but this one’s a way better buy for almost everybody.) For the same $550 you’ll drop on the 12 Pro, you can get a base-model iPad with 256GB of storage. I’d probably tell you to buy the iPad; it has much better tablet software and much better big-screen apps, and Apple has a much better track record in tablets.

And yet for the last few days, I’ve had an iPad and an Alexa Tablet sitting on my desk, and every time I want to watch or read something I’ve found myself gravitating to Amazon’s device. It is really nice to look at.

We have to talk about this screen. It’s the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It’s a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls “Nanomatte” that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen.

The $549.99 device I’ve been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you don’t really need. The pitch for all those devices is the same: They’re well-made, midrange tablets that can access the full universe of Android apps through the Play Store and come with a whole bunch of Amazon bloatware whether you want it or not. I haven’t tested those other devices, but I’m glad they exist — cheap, good Android tablets are too hard to come by.

Amazon bloatware everywhereAlexa Plus isn’t greatSome middling specs

But the Nanomatte. The Nanomatte! The etching on the display, which Amazon says it partnered with Corning to do at a sub-pixel level to reduce glare without causing the slight rainbow-shimmering effect you can get on other matte screens, absolutely does its job. When I use my iPad outdoors, I can often see what’s behind me like I’m staring into a mirror; the 12 Pro reflects only a small sheen of light, and does it without losing any sharpness. The viewing angles are incredible, too. I’d like the display to be a little brighter, but since the main reason to crank the brightness is to fight glare, it hasn’t really been a problem.

The screen is not perfect. The anti-glare texture gives the Alexa Tablet a bit of shimmer, especially when you’re looking at light text on a black background. And the iPad’s blacks are still blacker; watching a movie, the letterboxes above and below are still slightly lit on the Alexa Tablet’s LCD, and they’re just flat-out off on the iPad’s OLED panel. Some of this you can fix: The 12 Pro has specific modes that automatically tweak tone and color to make reading more pleasant, and you can even control the overall picture through a few presets like the ones you’d find on your TV. My review unit came with “Boosted” mode turned on, which made every color just a smidge too colorful. I turned it to “Natural” and immediately liked the picture better.

I’m not sure this screen counts as some revolution in display technology, but then again, I did reflexively say “whoa” the first second I turned it on, and all that was showing was the Amazon logo. I like this display for everything. The 120Hz refresh rate looks great when running Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and the 3:2 aspect ratio feels right for web browsing and side-by-side work. The more muted display modes even make reading more pleasant than your average giant screen, though it’s lame that they only work in the Kindle app. After a few days of using the tablet indoors and out, I prefer the 12 Pro’s screen to any iPad I’ve tried. (Unfortunately, I don’t have an iPad Pro with the nano-texture glass to compare it to, but that’s a $2,200 tablet. I doubt anyone’s debating between the two.)

All that display tech in a $549.99 device requires tradeoffs basically everywhere else, and Amazon makes lots of them. The MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor benchmarks somewhere between a flagship high-end Android phone from last year and a flagship phone from two years ago, and gets absolutely lapped by practically every current iPad. In one graphics-heavy benchmark, the current 13-inch iPad Pro scored about nine times higher.

I’d like more horsepower here, but in my day-to-day use there’s plenty of power in this tablet. In several days of playing games, doing work, and watching a lot of NFL RedZone, the only slowness I’ve detected has been little niggling things in the Android experience. The app switcher sometimes stutters when it loads. I suppose I worry a little about how this tablet will age, given that it doesn’t share the iPad’s preposterous oversupply of processing power, but for now it’s fine.

Come to think of it, “it’s fine” explains most of the 12 Pro’s hardware. The four speakers are a little thin and muddy, but loud and clear enough. The cameras wash out some colors, but they work for video calls. The $149.99 keyboard case is nice to type on, but a little awkward to detach and manipulate. The $89.99 pen is smooth and responsive, but not many Android apps support a stylus. The battery lasts me about eight hours of screen time, which is a little less than I’d like and less than Amazon advertises. Nothing here is a deal-breaker, it’s just a lot of fine.

The software, on the other hand, is all extremes. The great news: The Alexa Tablets run full Android, not the weird off-brand operating system Amazon’s Fire tablets have used for the last 15 years. That means you get all the apps in the Play Store, a vastly improved interface, and access to things like Google’s Gemini assistant. All by itself, that change makes these the most functional Amazon tablets ever.

If you’re going to say you “obsess over customers,” you don’t get to borrow the top left corner of my homescreen and then use that space to show me an ad vaguely offering to “Cook with premium ingredients” that launches an also unhideable Alexa chat window in the bottom right corner of my homescreen.

Luckily, this is Android, and installing a new launcher takes 30 seconds. If you buy an Alexa Tablet, I recommend doing so immediately.

I would be less annoyed by Alexa’s overbearing presence on this tablet if Alexa Plus were actually useful, which it mostly is not. If you’re looking to buy whatever’s on your screen, Alexa’s your bot: You can invoke the assistant in any app, and it’ll almost always assume your goal is to shop for whatever you’re currently looking at. If you want, well, anything else, you’re probably out of luck. Almost a year after its launch, Alexa Plus is not a very good assistant. It’s slow, it gets lost in back-and-forth conversations, and it still doesn’t have enough access to my apps and data to be useful. You can switch to Gemini in the device’s settings, and you should.

Once you de-Amazon the tablet, you’re left with a pretty useful Android device. And this is where the Alexa Tablet gets tricky to evaluate. I wouldn’t recommend using it as a primary computer, given the still sorry state of large-screen Android apps. (Between this and the ongoing Googlebook fiasco, I really hope Google is learning a lesson about incentivizing developers to care about big screens and keyboards.) But between the Kindle-specific display mode, all the streaming and reading apps in the Play Store, and this terrific screen, this is immediately one of the best tablets-for-tablet-things you can buy.

Realistically, you’re probably debating whether to buy the Alexa Tablet or an iPad. (Apologies to the Samsung Galaxy Tab shoppers out there, but this one’s a way better buy for almost everybody.) For the same $550 you’ll drop on the 12 Pro, you can get a base-model iPad with 256GB of storage. I’d probably tell you to buy the iPad; it has much better tablet software and much better big-screen apps, and Apple has a much better track record in tablets.

And yet for the last few days, I’ve had an iPad and an Alexa Tablet sitting on my desk, and every time I want to watch or read something I’ve found myself gravitating to Amazon’s device. It is really nice to look at.

news.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
news.title_en: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
news.author: Ars Technica
news.article_content:
AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown.

By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.

Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own

news.title: Harmonic Security, which uses small language models to inspect employee interactions with AI tools, raised a $50M Series B, taking its total funding to $76M (Duncan Riley/SiliconANGLE)
news.title_en: Harmonic Security, which uses small language models to inspect employee interactions with AI tools, raised a $50M Series B, taking its total funding to $76M (Duncan Riley/SiliconANGLE)
news.author: SiliconANGLE
news.article_content:
SHARE


	
	
		
			
				
					
						UPDATED 08:00 EDT / OCTOBER 14 2026

Workplace artificial intelligence security startup Harmonic Security Inc. today announced it has raised $50 million in new funding to grow its platform for governing how employees use AI tools.

The company’s platform inspects anything an employee sends to an AI tool at work before it gets there. Custom small language models read each interaction in context, and a verdict comes back within milliseconds. Live credentials pasted into a chat window are one example of what the system is tuned to catch, according to Harmonic. A developer referencing a database schema should pass.

Those checks originally ran only in the browser, and over the past year Harmonic has extended them to desktop AI applications and agentic workflows. In Harmonic’s view, those tools are where problems such as employees signing in to AI services with personal accounts tend to start.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Alastair Paterson said “every board I talk to” now wants to know whether AI is delivering value, on top of how to reduce the risk of using it. Harmonic’s answer is a Usage Intelligence layer that runs on the same models. Leaders can see which AI use cases are paying off, down to individual employees who have worked out a faster way to get their jobs done.

Outside its own platform, Harmonic has been plugging into tools enterprises already use. Agent Builder, which Cisco Systems Inc. announced for its Cloud Control platform at Cisco Live in June, lists Harmonic among its ecosystem integrations. The connection runs over Model Context Protocol.

A second integration, with the Claude Compliance API from Anthropic PBC, pulls activity logs from Anthropic-hosted Claude Platform deployments into Harmonic. Organizations on Claude Enterprise also get the content of conversations.

More than 100 companies are customers, some of them among the largest enterprises in the world, and Harmonic said millions of their employees are covered. Climb Global Solutions Inc. and Distology Ltd. have signed on as distribution partners. Staff numbers have passed 90 across the U.S. and the U.K., and the new money will pay for more engineering and go-to-market hires on both sides of the Atlantic.

Security “has too often slowed the adoption of new technology,” according to Zach Sivertson, a managing director at Crosspoint. Organizations taking up AI should not have to give up control to move quickly, he said, adding that Harmonic gives leaders the visibility to roll AI out sooner.

Paterson said the company has “real momentum” and that the round lets it build faster as the AI market keeps changing. Investors have now put $76 million into Harmonic.

news.title: Alleged OpenAI spy vibe-coded a surveillance device using his wife's chatbot account
news.title_en: Alleged OpenAI spy vibe-coded a surveillance device using his wife's chatbot account
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
A Saudi national working as an engineer at OpenAI was arrested for allegedly planting an audio recording device, wrapped in toilet paper, inside the company's executive conference room. According to the indictment, he built the spy tool by vibe-coding it with a chatbot. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison.

The article Alleged OpenAI spy vibe-coded a surveillance device using his wife's chatbot account appeared first on The Decoder.

In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.

The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.

FBI officers fear the scenario is set to repeat itself: “Threat actors will likely increase their use of GenAI tools for attack planning,” said the memo, which was distributed by the bureau’s Los Angeles division in May 2026. “Current built-in GenAI safeguards are insufficient to prevent illicit use as malicious actors successfully employ ‘jailbreaking’ techniques to access dangerous information.”

AI executives and staff at leading AI companies have focused their public remarks on potential doomsday scenarios, a long-term, hypothetical harm of the technology they’re developing. Law enforcement officers, by contrast, have been grappling with what they fear are the present-day threats that AI enables, including violent crimes.

A previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists. Law enforcement has been trying to keep pace with the ways bad actors may be using AI for harm, concerned that the rapidly evolving technology may supercharge new and existing types of crimes.

At the same time, as public sentiment over AI and its impacts on society and the environment has soured, agencies have sought to protect AI infrastructure. The documents show police and intelligence officers are closely monitoring online opposition to datacenters among various groups with what they describe as extremist ideologies.

How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new members

How AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM)

How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detection

How to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these tools

Monitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacenters

The FBI did not respond to detailed questions on its monitoring of anti-AI sentiment and use of AI, but pointed to a general fact sheet on the agency’s use of the technology.

The NYPD stated that its threat analysis report on artificial intelligence was related to the “AI 2027” project – an influential forecast from several AI researchers that speculated about the technology’s rapid growth and the threats it could present. In one of the project’s possible futures, it predicted bioweapon-armed drones wiping out humanity.

“This NYPD Intelligence Analysis Report contained a summary and assessment of AI 2027,” the NYPD said. “It was distributed to appropriate NYPD members and partners for their awareness, as part of the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau’s mission of analyzing developments and trends that have implications for public safety and national security.”

DHS said it “prioritizes the safety and security of Americans and remains committed to mitigating all forms of ideologically-motivated violence”, and regularly shares intelligence with state and local law enforcement related to threats from violent extremists.

“DHS threat assessments draw on available intelligence, law-enforcement information, and other reporting to inform partners of evolving threats,” DHS said in a statement. “DHS assesses that malicious actors may seek to use artificial intelligence to enhance existing harmful activities, including cyber-enabled activity, fraud schemes, and the production or dissemination of violent extremist propaganda”.

Law enforcement’s concerns over AI and extremism fall into two broad categories, the documents show. One focuses on the burgeoning threat of extremists using new tools such as generative AI to plot attacks or promote their ideology. The other involves extremists targeting the modern technology that underpins society and has a long history within far-right movements.

Before mainstream, widespread opposition to datacenters swept the US, there was a strain of violent extremism that targeted tech facilities and other critical infrastructure, hoping such terrorism could lead to the collapse of society and instigate a race war.

Law enforcement officers expressed concern over the threat these militias posed to datacenters’ security before the 2022 launch of ChatGPT. Several bulletins, such as an October 2021 joint threat analysis from DHS, National Counterterrorism Center and FBI, highlighted a plot by Seth Pendley, a January 6 rioter and far-right militia member, to blow up an Amazon Web Services facility.

“Pendley believed a successful attack on the Amazon facility would disrupt 70 percent of Internet service, expose perceived abuses of power, and lead to revolution,” the bulletin said. Pendley pleaded guilty to a charge of malicious attempt to destroy a building with an explosive and was sentenced in 2021 to 10 years in prison for plotting the attack.

Although law enforcement has long tracked extremist militia threats to infrastructure like Pendley’s, the documents show that in the years since the generative AI boom began, agencies more frequently expressed concern over anti-tech and anti-datacenter sentiment. Multiple fusion centers – law enforcement hubs for collecting information and coordinating between agencies – around the US warned of growing threats from domestic violent extremists – pointing to posts across social media platforms, messaging apps and forums like 4chan in which commenters vowed to destroy datacenters.

“I bring a sort of ‘tannerite and gasoline’ vibe to ai data centers,” an account associated with a white supremacist posted on Facebook last year, according to a 2025 Philadelphia police department intelligence bulletin. Combining gasoline with Tannerite, a brand of well-known explosive compound, produces a large and fiery detonation.

On some far-right forums, users discussed killing CEOs of AI companies and local officials who support datacenters, agents warned, as well as arson and bombing attacks against data facilities.

Law enforcement also monitored real-world anti-datacenter incidents or protests, including a demonstration in Michigan in March where the documents said that three people allegedly associated with a white supremacist group held a banner opposing what they called a “Jewish data center” being built in the state.

As opposition to artificial intelligence and datacenters have become more widespread, however, questions have risen over how law enforcement agencies’ tracking anti-datacenter and anti-tech ideology may bleed over into surveillance of nonviolent protest movements. Distrust of the AI industry and mobilization against datacenters has now become so prevalent that it is a mainstream issue of the midterm elections, far from an extremist position.

The documents show agencies casting a wide net as they track opposition to the tech industry, including broadly monitoring public social media and opposition such as proposed legislation against datacenters. In a Nevada Threat Analysis Center report from April 2026, law enforcement cited a local city council hearing on a datacenter moratorium as part of a trend of increased negative sentiment towards the facilities.

Some experts and activists have expressed concern that as mobilization against datacenters grows, peaceful anti-AI organizations could face surveillance from authorities.

“There’s nothing extreme about not wanting to lose your livelihood to AI, your drinking water to AI datacenters, your privacy to ubiquitous AI surveillance or your life to runaway rogue AI,” said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People. “What’s extreme is the law enforcement treating these legitimate objections as threats to be neutralized.”

In the months after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in 2022, law enforcement across the US began to pay attention to the way the novel technology was being used. Even in its infancy, the tool could produce images that were indistinguishable from “authentic images”, according to one May 2023 law enforcement document. Police in Minnesota and in California worried that function could exacerbate problems with child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and “terrorist propaganda materials”.

At the time, many of these risks were largely theoretical in the eyes of law enforcement, the documents show. In one memo distributed by two California intelligence centers, officials warned that officers should remain vigilant because they predicted AI may one day make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, that it may be used to produce and disseminate deepfakes and that it may increase the volume of propaganda.

In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.

The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.

FBI officers fear the scenario is set to repeat itself: “Threat actors will likely increase their use of GenAI tools for attack planning,” said the memo, which was distributed by the bureau’s Los Angeles division in May 2026. “Current built-in GenAI safeguards are insufficient to prevent illicit use as malicious actors successfully employ ‘jailbreaking’ techniques to access dangerous information.”

AI executives and staff at leading AI companies have focused their public remarks on potential doomsday scenarios, a long-term, hypothetical harm of the technology they’re developing. Law enforcement officers, by contrast, have been grappling with what they fear are the present-day threats that AI enables, including violent crimes.

A previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists. Law enforcement has been trying to keep pace with the ways bad actors may be using AI for harm, concerned that the rapidly evolving technology may supercharge new and existing types of crimes.

At the same time, as public sentiment over AI and its impacts on society and the environment has soured, agencies have sought to protect AI infrastructure. The documents show police and intelligence officers are closely monitoring online opposition to datacenters among various groups with what they describe as extremist ideologies.

How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new members

How AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM)

How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detection

How to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these tools

Monitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacenters

The FBI did not respond to detailed questions on its monitoring of anti-AI sentiment and use of AI, but pointed to a general fact sheet on the agency’s use of the technology.

The NYPD stated that its threat analysis report on artificial intelligence was related to the “AI 2027” project – an influential forecast from several AI researchers that speculated about the technology’s rapid growth and the threats it could present. In one of the project’s possible futures, it predicted bioweapon-armed drones wiping out humanity.

“This NYPD Intelligence Analysis Report contained a summary and assessment of AI 2027,” the NYPD said. “It was distributed to appropriate NYPD members and partners for their awareness, as part of the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau’s mission of analyzing developments and trends that have implications for public safety and national security.”

DHS said it “prioritizes the safety and security of Americans and remains committed to mitigating all forms of ideologically-motivated violence”, and regularly shares intelligence with state and local law enforcement related to threats from violent extremists.

“DHS threat assessments draw on available intelligence, law-enforcement information, and other reporting to inform partners of evolving threats,” DHS said in a statement. “DHS assesses that malicious actors may seek to use artificial intelligence to enhance existing harmful activities, including cyber-enabled activity, fraud schemes, and the production or dissemination of violent extremist propaganda”.

Law enforcement’s concerns over AI and extremism fall into two broad categories, the documents show. One focuses on the burgeoning threat of extremists using new tools such as generative AI to plot attacks or promote their ideology. The other involves extremists targeting the modern technology that underpins society and has a long history within far-right movements.

Before mainstream, widespread opposition to datacenters swept the US, there was a strain of violent extremism that targeted tech facilities and other critical infrastructure, hoping such terrorism could lead to the collapse of society and instigate a race war.

Law enforcement officers expressed concern over the threat these militias posed to datacenters’ security before the 2022 launch of ChatGPT. Several bulletins, such as an October 2021 joint threat analysis from DHS, National Counterterrorism Center and FBI, highlighted a plot by Seth Pendley, a January 6 rioter and far-right militia member, to blow up an Amazon Web Services facility.

“Pendley believed a successful attack on the Amazon facility would disrupt 70 percent of Internet service, expose perceived abuses of power, and lead to revolution,” the bulletin said. Pendley pleaded guilty to a charge of malicious attempt to destroy a building with an explosive and was sentenced in 2021 to 10 years in prison for plotting the attack.

Although law enforcement has long tracked extremist militia threats to infrastructure like Pendley’s, the documents show that in the years since the generative AI boom began, agencies more frequently expressed concern over anti-tech and anti-datacenter sentiment. Multiple fusion centers – law enforcement hubs for collecting information and coordinating between agencies – around the US warned of growing threats from domestic violent extremists – pointing to posts across social media platforms, messaging apps and forums like 4chan in which commenters vowed to destroy datacenters.

“I bring a sort of ‘tannerite and gasoline’ vibe to ai data centers,” an account associated with a white supremacist posted on Facebook last year, according to a 2025 Philadelphia police department intelligence bulletin. Combining gasoline with Tannerite, a brand of well-known explosive compound, produces a large and fiery detonation.

On some far-right forums, users discussed killing CEOs of AI companies and local officials who support datacenters, agents warned, as well as arson and bombing attacks against data facilities.

Law enforcement also monitored real-world anti-datacenter incidents or protests, including a demonstration in Michigan in March where the documents said that three people allegedly associated with a white supremacist group held a banner opposing what they called a “Jewish data center” being built in the state.

As opposition to artificial intelligence and datacenters have become more widespread, however, questions have risen over how law enforcement agencies’ tracking anti-datacenter and anti-tech ideology may bleed over into surveillance of nonviolent protest movements. Distrust of the AI industry and mobilization against datacenters has now become so prevalent that it is a mainstream issue of the midterm elections, far from an extremist position.

The documents show agencies casting a wide net as they track opposition to the tech industry, including broadly monitoring public social media and opposition such as proposed legislation against datacenters. In a Nevada Threat Analysis Center report from April 2026, law enforcement cited a local city council hearing on a datacenter moratorium as part of a trend of increased negative sentiment towards the facilities.

Some experts and activists have expressed concern that as mobilization against datacenters grows, peaceful anti-AI organizations could face surveillance from authorities.

“There’s nothing extreme about not wanting to lose your livelihood to AI, your drinking water to AI datacenters, your privacy to ubiquitous AI surveillance or your life to runaway rogue AI,” said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People. “What’s extreme is the law enforcement treating these legitimate objections as threats to be neutralized.”

In the months after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in 2022, law enforcement across the US began to pay attention to the way the novel technology was being used. Even in its infancy, the tool could produce images that were indistinguishable from “authentic images”, according to one May 2023 law enforcement document. Police in Minnesota and in California worried that function could exacerbate problems with child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and “terrorist propaganda materials”.

At the time, many of these risks were largely theoretical in the eyes of law enforcement, the documents show. In one memo distributed by two California intelligence centers, officials warned that officers should remain vigilant because they predicted AI may one day make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, that it may be used to produce and disseminate deepfakes and that it may increase the volume of propaganda.

news.title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
news.title_en: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.

Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.

The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.

news.title: My Friend Has No Soul
news.title_en: My Friend Has No Soul
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.

“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”

“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”

You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.

Courtesy of FriendFriend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.

The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.

The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.

It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.

When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.

Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.

ArrowI dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.

When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”

“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”

Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.

I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.

“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”

It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.

That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.

"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."

The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.

"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”

“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

news.title: China's industrial dominance is driven by competitive local governments that act like venture capital firms, making it a continent-sized Silicon Valley (Works in Progress Magazine)
news.title_en: China's industrial dominance is driven by competitive local governments that act like venture capital firms, making it a continent-sized Silicon Valley (Works in Progress Magazine)
news.author: Works in Progress Magazine
news.article_content:
This is only a slight caricature of how city government works in China. Provincial cities like Hefei and Hangzhou have become world-leading centers of commerce in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, solar panels, batteries, and AI, steered by mayors whose career incentives are similar to those of partners in a venture capital firm, getting promoted if their portfolio grows and fired if it fails. The cities they run function as vertically integrated conglomerates that benefit not just from the success of their local champions, but also from the broader growth generated by masses of companies in their slipstream.

The heavy state involvement correctly perceived by observers belongs not to Beijing but to those local governments, of which China has thousands, and which compete with one another for investment and prestige. These local growth machines and the competition between them are what drives China’s stunning economic success, and what the Western world must embrace to keep up.

For the initial decades after China’s economic opening in the 1980s, ‘Made in China’ meant cheap goods mass-produced for Western businesses. Today, Chinese companies lead the world in high-tech manufacturing, and many of them are household names in the West. Huawei is arguably the world’s most advanced telecoms company; BYD is the largest electric automaker; and DJI makes over 90 percent of consumer drones. Less familiar but no less important are companies like Geely, an auto giant which began in the 1980s as a refrigerator parts manufacturer and now owns Volvo, Lotus, Polestar and a stake in Aston Martin; and Vivo, now India’s biggest smartphone supplier.

What all have in common is that Beijing played no role in their creation. They were private companies encouraged by local governments. Huawei, BYD, and DJI emerged from Shenzhen’s Special Economic Zone, where municipal bureaucrats could write local regulations without regard for national rules. Geely was quietly supported by Zhejiang province at a time when only state-designated automakers were meant to build cars. Vivo spun off from a company founded in Dongguan, after Zhongshan, the neighboring city, wouldn’t give the company leaders equity.

Some sectors, such as batteries, electronics, and most recently electric vehicles, have received special support from Beijing as strategic industries. Companies in these areas benefited from subsidies, tax rebates, and in the case of electric cars, sales tax exemptions. But though the state was happy to lend its support to certain sectors, it was agnostic as to which specific firms and regions rose to dominance by means of that support. Beijing set a prize, and local bureaucrats competed to win it.

Hefei, the capital of Anhui province in inland Eastern China, is the most famous illustration of this process in action. In 2008, the municipal government invested $500 million in the electronic display company BOE Technology to build a new-generation LCD production line, bringing China to the cutting edge of panel production for the first time. At the time, Hefei was an unremarkable city with no display industry, and BOE was only the world’s ninth-largest manufacturer of LCD displays. The city provided the necessary land, utility connections, and cheap capital (investing almost a tenth of its total revenue that year) to set up a subsidiary company with BOE, in which it had an 81 percent stake. The bet paid off. BOE is now the world’s largest display panel manufacturer and makes about a quarter of smartphone screens worldwide.

The city reinvested the returns from its investment in other venture capital–like bets, which have won big surprisingly often. Hefei’s investment in carmaker NIO, which the city backed in 2020 in exchange for a 24 percent stake, paid off with an internal rate of return exceeding 30 percent. CXMT (Changxin Memory Technologies), 24 percent of which is directly or indirectly owned by the city of Hefei, runs just behind Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron with 7 percent of the global market for DRAM chips, the short-term memory used in smartphones, PCs, and data centers. Over the decade to 2023, the city had invested roughly $25 billion of public funds, generating reported earnings of nearly $9 billion.

Other cities have followed the venture capital model to bring in similar growth in jobs and tax revenues. The city of Wuhu imported a secondhand Ford engine line from Britain, lured engineers away from state behemoth FAW (First Automotive Works), and copied a Volkswagen design to build a local carmaker. That makeshift venture eventually grew into Chery, today one of the country’s leading carmakers and supplier of Britain’s bestselling car in March 2026, the Jaecoo 7. As well as having seen growth in jobs, exports, and tax revenues, the city of Wuhu retains a 21 percent stake in Chery, worth around $3.7 billion.

Ningde, a relatively modest city in Fujian province in the southeast, is the founding site of CATL, now the world’s biggest battery producer. The city’s leaders made a strategic wager from its founding in 2011, committing land, infrastructure, tax support, administrative coordination, and supplier attraction efforts to help the still-young battery company to scale. CATL’s bases in Ningde now have capacity to produce 330 gigawatt hours of batteries per year – equivalent to almost half the global demand for electric vehicle batteries in 2023.

China’s mayors and provincial governors turn their cities into venture capital portfolios because of the system of incentives in which they operate. 2 Each cadre (the party members and other officials who run the Chinese state) is scored by their superiors in a secret file built up over the course of their career. Prefecture-level party secretaries evaluate county chiefs, who in turn evaluate their juniors heading up townships, who evaluate village leaders, down to the lowest party member.

Promotions – not just for politicians, but across the civil service – are based in large part on scoring the economic performance of the province or city that a cadre is responsible for. For example, the Shaoxing Municipal Party Committee’s 2008 assessment for city leaders featured 100 base points, of which 54 were awarded for economic development, including growth in GDP per capita, local revenue, industrial investment, and exports. A cadre must make the jump from county officialdom to prefecture level by their mid-forties, must take the next jump to provincial or ministerial level by their mid-fifties, and is unlikely ever to reach the Politburo if they have not done so by their sixties. Missing an age window means being locked into a lower tier for the rest of their lives.

What makes these incentives work is the fact that, unlike in many Western systems, provincial governments get to keep much of the money they generate. Li started at the bottom: he was born in 1959 to an unremarkable family in Rui’an, an ancient but small city in Zhejiang province, and worked factory clerk jobs before joining the local branch of the Communist Party in 1983. In 2002, he was made party secretary of Wenzhou, a larger city in the same province. Even under communism, Wenzhou had been seen as an outpost of entrepreneurship and private business within Zhejiang. Li described his strategy as getting the government out of the way to ‘allow the market to play its decisive role, further stimulating the entrepreneurial and innovative drive of the masses’. In practice this meant scrapping 8,000 of the province’s legal powers, including over 700 approval requirements.

Being a local government bureaucrat is a very different proposition in China than it is in the West. China’s public servants are more like company directors than administrators, making investments to increase their division’s financial performance and improve their professional prospects.

Competition is the driving force of Chinese industrial success. Instead of a single body making decisions for the entire country and passing them down, there are hundreds. When a strategy is proven to work, the country doubles down on it. In this, it is similar to American capitalism, with its hedge funds, investment banks, and venture capitalists, each a competitive central planner, portioning out capital for a sliver of the United States economy.

But China takes it further. In American capitalism, each individual ‘player’ represents their own interests, but nobody represents the interests of the game as a whole, which often makes coordination problems hard to solve. China’s competitive municipal socialism works because of local governments’ role as, effectively, landowners. Because they capture the spillovers of growth through rising land values and tax receipts, local governments create public goods that benefit all the companies in their area.

Local governments in the West have many of the tools that China’s cities have, but they lack the same incentives. Its cities suffer from fragmented political governance, like the San Francisco Bay Area, which is governed by 101 different municipal governments, or from rules that cap or redistribute their property tax revenues. Many Western cities have become dysfunctional even when they host economic clusters that rival those in China.

In contrast, China’s governments retain a large share of the money they raise and are led by cadres whose careers depend on growth. They have both the tools and the incentives to build their economic clusters up as much as they can. Sometimes this means directly luring in anchor firms which attract other companies to the area through tax rebates, specific infrastructure offers, and cheap bank loans.

To bring Tesla to Shanghai, the municipal government under Li Qiang offered $289 million in grants, arranged for $2.2 billion in low-interest loans from Chinese banks, a ten-point cut in the corporate income tax rate from 2019 to 2023, and a 50 percent discount on the 86 hectares of land beneath the factory. The support was so lavish that one Chinese minister reportedly complained that ‘Shanghai leaders were unbelievable – giving away the entire investment without Tesla having to spend a penny.’

Li promised speed along with capital. Elon Musk thought the factory would take two years to build; Li promised to do it in one. Tesla set up a Shanghai-based subsidiary in May 2018, signed a deal with the city in July, contracted for the land it needed in October, began construction in January 2019, and started producing cars in December that year. Even by Musk’s standards, Shanghai’s processes were lightning fast. Retooling an existing factory in Fremont, California, took Tesla almost twice as long, and building a new Berlin gigafactory took almost three times as long. Musk himself credited the Shanghai government as essential for that speed.

Sometimes, as in Hefei, support even means making direct investments that help anchor companies to grow as well as providing equity returns directly to the city’s coffers. Chinese provinces and cities make heavy use of cash subsidies, which total 2 percent of Chinese GDP according to the IMF, compared to around 0.3 percent in the United States and 0.5 percent in the European Union.

These direct inducements and investments are an important part of the puzzle. But these investments would not pay off if cities were not prepared to capitalize on them. Chinese cities are. They zone masses of land for industry, rent it out at a cut price to build the larger cluster around the anchor firms, then fund the discount by selling land to developers who lease it to the workers and entrepreneurs attracted in.

Kunshan, a small city near Shanghai, was a poor place – known as the ‘little sixth’ for being the least developed of the six subdivisions in its region – when, without permission from Beijing, its leaders secretly started an industrial zone in the mid-1980s. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Kunshan’s officials courted Taiwanese electronics firms with almost comic enthusiasm, building a Taiwanese school, encouraging Taiwanese restaurants, broadcasting forty Taiwanese TV channels, and offering industrial land at throwaway prices. Nantz and Foxconn were among the first Taiwanese companies to arrive, making boring but foundational parts like electrical connectors and printed circuit boards. By the late 2000s, Kunshan made half of all  laptops in the world.

Danyang, in Jiangsu, hosts 1,600 companies that manufacture half the world’s spectacle lenses. In a remarkable range of specialized manufacturing sectors, both light and heavy, a Chinese hub holds a world-dominant position.
