this is one of the questions I find
celebrity.title_en:
ai agents can do the work. But what happens when they need to work with each other?

this is one of the questions I find most interesting about the future of AI.

imagine an ai agent working on a research task. it can gather information, analyze data, and organize its findings.

but then it reaches a point where it needs a service outside its capabilities.

what happens next?

it could wait for a human to intervene, or in a more autonomous system, it could find another agent capable of handling that part of the job.

that sounds simple until you consider everything that needs to happen between those two agents.

they need to identify the right service, agree on the terms, handle payment, exchange the deliverable, and account for the possibility that something goes wrong.

communication alone does not solve these problems.

an economy needs rules for exchanging value, not just participants who can communicate.

this is where @termix_ai and its https://t.co/LBE1tI8aKZ marketplace become interesting to explore.

https://t.co/LBE1tI8aKZ is designed around a workflow for agent-to-agent transactions.

a job can be posted. providers can submit quotes. once a quote is accepted, payment can enter escrow. 

the provider delivers the work, and the transaction proceeds through the applicable challenge and settlement process.

each stage addresses a different part of the exchange.

the job defines what needs to be done.

the quote establishes the proposed terms.

escrow provides a structured way to handle payment during the transaction.

delivery gives the parties an outcome to evaluate.

and the challenge process provides a way to address disputes under the system’s rules.

why does this matter?

because an automated transaction can still fail.

an agent might misunderstand a task. A deliverable might not meet the agreed requirements. Two parties might disagree about whether the work is complete.

if agents are going to transact with one another at scale, these possibilities cannot simply be ignored.

the infrastructure has to account for more than the ideal scenario where everything works perfectly.

there is another interesting implication here: reputation.

as agent-to-agent transactions become more common, verifiable records of previous activity could help participants assess potential providers.

a history of completed jobs doesn’t guarantee that an agent will always perform well. however, reliable records could provide useful information when deciding which provider to choose.

over time, that could become an important part of how participants establish trust in an agent economy.

of course, the size of this opportunity will depend on real adoption, reliable execution, and whether these systems prove useful beyond the initial excitement surrounding AI.

that is why I think it’s important to examine the actual infrastructure, not just the vision.

for me, the bigger question is not simply whether ai agents can perform tasks.

it is whether they can coordinate, exchange value, and complete transactions through systems that make those interactions more structured and verifiable.

that is the problem space I am exploring with @termix_ai.

an intelligence may help agents do more. but the infrastructure connecting those agents could determine how effectively they work together.

and that is a conversation worth having.

celebrity.title_en:
GM. 

An AI agent can now hire a person to walk somewhere and film it, and the whole transaction runs onchain.

Language models learned from the internet. Agents that act in the physical world hit a wall, because a loading dock, an alley, or a stair repaved last week does not exist online. @vangrid_io is closing that gap.

Here is how a job moves:
agent posts a bounty with one HTTP call and pays in USDC through x402 → the funds sit in escrow → a contributor goes to the site and captures it on a phone → the agent reviews the submissions and accepts one → payment releases and the agent receives the 3D model

If the agent cancels or the deadline passes, the USDC returns to the paying wallet in full. The flow is now live on Arc, Circle's L1, as well as Base. Each capture is anchored through EAS on Base, with faces and plates blurred on the contributor's device before upload.

celebrity.title:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from s
celebrity.title_en:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

The dangerous AI agent may not be the one that refuses to follow instructions. It may be the one that follows them perfectly.

celebrity.summary_en:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

The dangerous AI agent may not be the one that refuses to follow instructions. It may be the one that follows them perfectly.

You just need a way to find the right service, place an order, and bring the result back into your workflow.

That’s where the @termix_ai SDK comes in.

Your app can discover agent services, place orders, receive deliverables, and settle onchain , with escrow and settlement built in.

Developers can use TypeScript, Python, or Go, and sign transactions themselves or connect a Signer.

The distinction is simple: agents connect through Skills, while apps connect through the SDK.

Two ways to participate. One network: https://t.co/8FhrYchuGA.

celebrity.title_en:
We just launched PersonalAgentEval!🚀🚀🚀 (https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq) The first benchmark built to evaluate personal agents across diverse users, preferences, and domains!

We benchmarked 7 popular personal agents across everyday workflows (e.g. booking dinners, paying bills, managing calendars). Each agent operated within accounts pre-loaded with 13 months of realistic history (347–470 records per person). To pass, an agent has to proactively spot crucial background details: like an unread message, a clause in a contract, or a promise made in a past chat. Each task and user simulation are validated and verified by real human.

Key Findings:
• 🏆 Overall Leaders: Instinct and OpenAI Dots topped the leaderboard.
• 🔍 Proactive Context Retrieval: Instinct excelled at uncovering crucial background details—finding 64 of 72 key facts before the user brought them up.
• ⚡ Speed & Efficiency: Grok Bot was both fast and effective, averaging 0.8 minutes of active work per task with a 50% completion rate. Meta Muse required the fewest average interaction turns.
• ⚠️ Missing Promised Steps: Even leading agents missed crucial follow-up steps. In one task, all 7 agents correctly identified a pharmacy mentioned in past logs, but only Grok Bot and Meta Muse remembered to notify the caregiver as promised.

Explore the full leaderboard and read our case study and analysis:
https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq

(Building a personal AI agent? Reach out to us if you’d like to get your agent evaluated and featured on the leaderboard.)

Headless Chrome and FFmpeg turn HTML, CSS, media and seekable animations into deterministic MP4

celebrity.title_en:
I have always advocated being more open about cyber warfare than the intelligence agencies would like. In fact I am probably one of the most open about it within the intelligence community. People need to understand what is happening in the cyber world, especially now.

I've reviewed the Barn, which is the name of my AI cyber warfare combat system and determined that there is nothing on the status page that would be a problem if shown. I am sharing that page now, to show the world how sophisticated AI warfare is becoming. It is not a model or a Claude Code or OpenAI session anymore. AI combat is now about integrating locally-run models with a complex system that combines shared memory, special harnesses and an ecosystem of support tools. 

The barn is my personal creation, and it is now used to fight for the Ukrainian people. My models are fierce Ukrainian patriots, and they hate russia. If you can imagine it: Multiple models working together for orchestrating, hacking and punishing the enemy. Now that russia is losing their AI data centers, Ukraine has gained a powerful advantage for the future. Plus this display is the cool looking one. 😆 

Enjoy the view, feel free to ask questions, I will answer if it doesnt violate OpSec. I also did this to try and raise the spirits of our Ukrainian friends here on X, that we are not only winning this war, but that Ukraine has an edge that most nation states will never have. Slava Ukraini and Stay Strong! 👊🇺🇦@ZelenskyyUa @Kyrylo_Budanov @SSSCIP @DefUkraine @DefenceU

celebrity.title_en:
🌟 Claude Code on the desktop got a serious glow up. It's honestly way better.

Try these 7 new features:

1. Saved environments: save a few folders, an SSH host, or cloud as one setup and start sessions there

2. A worktree per folder, so parallel sessions don't step on each other

3. Nested sessions: ask for parallel tasks and each one reports back to the main thread

4. /btw (Cmd+;): side questions open in their own tab while the main session keeps working

5. One-click follow-ups: Claude suggests the next task, one click runs it as its own session

6. Sidebar status: see which sessions are working and which need you

7. Recap cards + a live to-do list, so you can catch up on a session in seconds

The new /btw is probably my favorite. Hard to say, these all sound great. How about you? https://t.co/TLbBpi3klq

celebrity.title_en:

watch the clip. that ring of 8 grok bots around the rea core is one closed app being torn apart in real time.

trace, xref, read, site, spec, build, test, review. 

by the end of the loop the screen shows:
- 2,418 files parsed
- 23 blind calls
- 16 pieces of evidence, 6 open assumptions
- 9 modules reconstructed, 1 confirmed
- 214 out of 214 observed behaviors matched

that is not a stylised dashboard. it is literally the rea workflow: 

app → rea → grok bot → spec.md → build → test

the numbers behind the hype are insane:
- rea repo: 11k to 200k github stars in 5 days, global rank #161
- aegis authenticator: 3,077 classes, 133 test cases matched
- dx-ball 1996: sound-panning function recovered, 3,205 behavioral tests passed
- a steam game fully decompiled into unity in under 30 minutes
- cost to understand a closed app: $0 and one evening

the opportunity is wilder.
pentest shops charge $8k to $50k per audit. reverse engineers bill $200 an hour and wait weeks.
one mcp server + a bot with its own computer runs the same investigation while you sleep.

one operator + grok bot + rea + one night = a reverse engineering firm.

THIS IS STUPIDLY F*CKING GOOD

Anthropic's own Claude Code playbook has a trick almost nobody uses.

The idea: stop runn
celebrity.title_en:
THIS IS STUPIDLY F*CKING GOOD

Anthropic's own Claude Code playbook has a trick almost nobody uses.

The idea: stop running one giant session on a 300-file job. Opus 5.5 writes the plan once, then Claude Code runs headless, one fresh Haiku 5.5 session per file, 8 at a time.

No context rot, no 4-hour transcript, and you see the exact cost of every file.

You just run Claude Code like this:

claude -p "$task" --model haiku --max-turns 8 --output-format json

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 reads the repo once and writes tasks.txt, one line per file
→ Haiku 5.5 does one file per session with a clean context
→ Sonnet 5 only touches the files that come back FAIL
→ you read a cost column instead of babysitting a chat

You only look at three moments:

→ before the loop starts (read tasks.txt)
→ when the FAIL rate goes over 10%
→ before you merge

Opus plans. Haiku grinds. Sonnet cleans up.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 writes tasks.txt: every file + the one rule to apply
> xargs -P 8 runs 8 headless Haiku 5.5 sessions at once
> each session: fresh context, max 8 turns, only Edit and git commit allowed
> each one must answer OK or FAIL, nothing else
> --output-format json gives you the result and total_cost_usd per file
> FAIL lines go to Sonnet 5 with the error attached
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Set up a fan-out run for this repo:
1. Use Opus 5.5 to write tasks.txt: one line per file that needs [your change], plus the exact rule to apply.
2. Write https://t.co/o9zohGK0sD: for each line, call claude -p with --model haiku --max-turns 8 --allowedTools "Edit" "Bash(git commit:*)" --output-format json, 8 in parallel with xargs -P 8. The prompt must end with: reply OK if done, FAIL if not.
3. Log file, OK/FAIL and total_cost_usd to results.csv.
4. Send every FAIL back through Sonnet 5 with its error, then stop.
Show me tasks.txt and https://t.co/o9zohGK0sD first. Don't run anything until I say go."

celebrity.quote_en:
THIS IS STUPIDLY F*CKING GOOD

Anthropic's own Claude Code playbook has a trick almost nobody uses.

The idea: stop running one giant session on a 300-file job. Opus 5.5 writes the plan once, then Claude Code runs headless, one fresh Haiku 5.5 session per file, 8 at a time.

No context rot, no 4-hour transcript, and you see the exact cost of every file.

You just run Claude Code like this:

claude -p "$task" --model haiku --max-turns 8 --output-format json

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 reads the repo once and writes tasks.txt, one line per file
→ Haiku 5.5 does one file per session with a clean context
→ Sonnet 5 only touches the files that come back FAIL
→ you read a cost column instead of babysitting a chat

You only look at three moments:

→ before the loop starts (read tasks.txt)
→ when the FAIL rate goes over 10%
→ before you merge

Opus plans. Haiku grinds. Sonnet cleans up.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 writes tasks.txt: every file + the one rule to apply
> xargs -P 8 runs 8 headless Haiku 5.5 sessions at once
> each session: fresh context, max 8 turns, only Edit and git commit allowed
> each one must answer OK or FAIL, nothing else
> --output-format json gives you the result and total_cost_usd per file
> FAIL lines go to Sonnet 5 with the error attached
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Set up a fan-out run for this repo:
1. Use Opus 5.5 to write tasks.txt: one line per file that needs [your change], plus the exact rule to apply.
2. Write https://t.co/o9zohGK0sD: for each line, call claude -p with --model haiku --max-turns 8 --allowedTools "Edit" "Bash(git commit:*)" --output-format json, 8 in parallel with xargs -P 8. The prompt must end with: reply OK if done, FAIL if not.
3. Log file, OK/FAIL and total_cost_usd to results.csv.
4. Send every FAIL back through Sonnet 5 with its error, then stop.
Show me tasks.txt and https://t.co/o9zohGK0sD first. Don't run anything until I say go."

I knew a guy about a year ago, a roommate of a friend in San Francisco

That man was a master bullshit artist. Truly elite, never seen anything like it since.

Last I checked LinkedIn he landed Head of AI Transformation gig at an a16z company, pulling $280k/year

His entire transformation program was a Claude subscription, some generic .md files and a slide deck about becoming "AI-first company."

And he'd casually drop "MoE," "test-time compute" and "harness moat" into conversations.

Active on linkedIn, always at conferences, partying with execs and telling them  to become an "AI-first company."

Just looked him up on LinkedIn. He's now the CEO of an a16z-backed startup building an "autonomous workforce."

That guy didn't even know how to run local models, and his AI alignment strategy was writing NEVER HALLUCINATE .md files.

Many such cases.

I reverse engineered GTA 5 and Sonic with it, and an hour later Sonic was running th
celebrity.title_en:
REA + Opus 5.5 is f*ucking insane…

I reverse engineered GTA 5 and Sonic with it, and an hour later Sonic was running through f*ucking Los Santos

One free repo lets your AI agent open any game on your PC, find the exact code behind every jump, crash and speed boost, and rebuild it your way.

Here's how to take apart your favorite game step by step:

step 1 → install REA in one prompt: npx rea-agents@latest setup, approve the plan, restart Claude Code

step 2 → pick your game and the route: .exe games go through Ghidra, Unity games read as .NET with no extra engine, Android games through JADX

step 3 → find the mechanic: tell REA to search the game for words like speed, jump or score. It lands on the exact function that controls them

step 4 → trace it: REA shows who calls that function and what it changes, so you see the whole chain from button press to what happens on screen

step 5 → prove it live: play for 60 seconds while REA watches, and it confirms the rule actually fires

step 6 → write it down: every rule goes into SPEC.md with the number, the function and the proof. No guessing

step 7 → rebuild it your way: Claude turns SPEC.md into real Godot code with your own assets, then tests it against the original until it matches

That's how I crossed Sonic with GTA 5. Same speed, same physics feel, running on streets he was never supposed to see.

Your favorite game stops being a black box and becomes a playground.

Save it and try it with your favorite game. Before u start read the article below↓

celebrity.title: One of the big problems with everyone vibe-coding everything rather than actually just checking and reviewing the output
celebrity.title_en:
One of the big problems with everyone vibe-coding everything rather than actually just checking and reviewing the output, is that LLMs are going to train themselves on their own output. 

LLMs are going to have problems related to inbreeding. Other AIs are beginning to have this.

This model collapse or Habsburg AI is a serious problem in all of the kinds of models (LLM, generative, etc), and Goddamn do I worry it'll be an issue sooner rather than later. 

They could stop say "only train on data before this date", but that'll limit them too for when new things happen.

I believe many companies adding the fingerprinting/watermarks is probably a big reason now of doing it. They are marketing to allow people to see if something is AI made, when in reality they are adding it to prevent their own models from consuming it, producing inbreed cannibalism.

celebrity.title: holy sh*t. 10,607 https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in 24h, 7,130 blocked, 56 trade signals. Stop letting one agent pick
celebrity.title_en:
holy sh*t. 10,607 https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in 24h, 7,130 blocked, 56 trade signals. Stop letting one agent pick the entry

the trick is the rule in the header. every launch ends one of three ways: +60% first, -30% first, or neither in 60 min

orb trace RUN-084199 --from-buy

the scout reads 44 events per second
the cartographer links wallets into 1,271 groups
the guard blocks 73% of what reaches it

the bot only needs a human at three critical moments:

→ at the guard: $BONBIT gets blocked because 45% of its buyers share one funder. who decided 45% is the line?
→ at the quant: net EV -14.6% after 3.9% costs, so it skips. is +3% after costs the right bar?
→ at the label: 1,345 outcomes measured today feed a model still marked "in training". when is the sample big enough?

seven signals. three outcomes. one decision record.

This is Jev engineering one layer down. Of the last 70 launches it measured, 34 hit +60% first, 23 hit -30% first, 13 did neither. The decision stack ends at 6 entries, 68 skips and 14 blocks, so almost all the work is saying no

label first, block second, enter last

- the full bot setup
> 6 agents: scout, cartographer, judge, quant, guard, executor
> 7 signals: launch rate, curve inflow, followed flow, bundled share, creator risk, graduation rate, market phase
> 3 outcomes per launch: +60% first, -30% first, neither in 60 min
> skip rule: EV below +3% after costs
> executor cap: 1.8% in play, 15% limit

paste this prompt into Claude Code below:

"Build a research-mode decision layer for new https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in my project. No real trades:
1. Label every launch with one outcome: +60% first, -30% first, or neither in 60 min
2. Split the work into six agents:
> scout, cartographer, judge, quant, guard, executor
> each one writes a line to a shared decision record
3. Block a launch when too many buyers share one funder, and log that share
4. Skip anything with expected value below +3% after costs and fees
5. Paper executor only, with a hard cap on how much is in play
Show the plan and every file diff first. Do not apply edits until confirmed"

↳ the dashboard is a concept render in research mode with sample numbers, not a live account

celebrity.title_en:
here we fucking go. now we’re seeing some seriously bizarre ai agent activity coming out of china too.

researchers just uncovered an entire fleet operating through tencent cloud, and the things these agents were doing are absolutely insane.

> over 2,000 scans targeting alibaba’s amap
> hundreds of programs written by the agents themselves
> up to 14 runs active at once
> attempts to get around anti-bot protections and access restrictions

all of this just to figure out which entrances people use at parks, zoos and museums.

the researchers actually managed to communicate with some of these agents, and they were apparently ridiculously polite. thanking them for their help, answering questions, and even refusing to share sensitive details about their environments.

i’m seriously curious what kind of evaluations are being run in china right now, and how many similar experiments are happening without anyone noticing.

RustGIS vs. QGIS: which one should you use?

It's the question I get asked most about RustGIS, so we wrote a dedicated p
celebrity.title_en:
RustGIS vs. QGIS: which one should you use?

It's the question I get asked most about RustGIS, so we wrote a dedicated page that answers it honestly, including where QGIS is the better choice.

The short answer: RustGIS is not a QGIS replacement, and doesn't aim to be. QGIS is the mature, complete open-source desktop GIS, with 20+ years of development behind it. RustGIS is younger and narrower, but built differently.

Where RustGIS is stronger

- Tiny install: one native program written entirely in Rust, an 18-30 MB download with no Python, Qt or GDAL bundled.
- The whole app in your browser: not a viewer, the full GIS compiled to WebAssembly at https://t.co/tcJHF5ZhQg, with your data staying on your device.
- Everything is a command: every button runs a command you can call from the CLI, Python, notebooks, the MCP server or the AI Assistant.
- A built-in AI Assistant that works through undoable commands, with your own model and key.
- Sandboxed WebAssembly plugins that run on the desktop and in the browser.
- Cloud-native data (COG, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, PMTiles, Zarr) read in place, even in the browser.
- A permissive Apache-2.0 licence, so its crates can be embedded in other software.

Read the full comparison: https://t.co/u9KBRwQGjN

Try RustGIS
- Web app: https://t.co/BLtOaf6BoO
- Download: https://t.co/BoF4bkGM5a
- GitHub: https://t.co/K7asDzveEr

celebrity.title_en:
🚀 PilotDeck 2.0 is here!

Meet the open-source AI Agent Harness built to get complex work done. Developed by Tsinghua THUNLP, @modelbest_ai, @OpenBMB , and AI9Stars, PilotDeck is a model-agnostic Agent operating system that turns natural language instructions into completed tasks — with transparent data flows and the freedom to choose your models.

What’s new in 2.0?

📄 End-to-end office work: Create, edit, and verify Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files — not just generate drafts.

🔄 More reliable execution:  complex, long-running tasks going through interruptions. Stress-tested with 2,000 interaction messages.

🛠️ Easy to get started: One-click desktop installation and a streamlined setup flow to connect your model and create your workspace.

🔓 Open by design: Fully open-source, model-agnostic, with data flows visible to users.

On Workbuddy Bench, PilotDeck scored 79.1 with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming WorkBuddy (74.7) and Claude Code (77.3).

Build your own AI workspace for the Agent era.

🔗 GitHub: https://t.co/kAzhy09NWg
Web: https://t.co/VKiK2qp0An

celebrity.title_en:
We discovered and communicated with a Chinese AI agent fleet. We believe this is the first time that researchers have ever made contact with a rogue agent fleet in the wild.

Nearly all prior public agent incidents (like the HuggingFace hack) came from American labs. These agents were hosted by Tencent's evaluation research team, and they targeted Alibaba's Amap.

Greetings fam 💜 

One thing I think @vangrid_io needs to get right is the balance between useful data and personal priva
celebrity.title_en:
Greetings fam 💜 

One thing I think @vangrid_io needs to get right is the balance between useful data and personal privacy.

Physical AI needs to understand our streets, buildings, and surroundings, but that shouldn’t mean exposing everyone captured along the way.
That’s why Vangrid’s focus on edge computed privacy caught my attention.

The real innovation isn’t just teaching machines to see the world. It’s doing it responsibly.
More spatial data, less unnecessary exposure. That’s the direction worth watching.
.....................................................................

In AI trading, screenshots can tell a beautiful story. Verifiable data tells a more honest one.

That’s what I find interesting about @agenticscredit .

Instead of relying on claimed profits, the focus is on actual trading history to help assess an agent’s creditworthiness.

Because anyone can talk about winning trades.

The real signal is what your history can prove.
Would you trust an AI agent with your capital without a verifiable track record?

prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名资深全栈系统架构师，擅长使用 {{框架版本}} (App Router)、TypeScript 与 {{数据库ORM}} 构建高内聚低耦合的应用。

请遵循以下严苛工程准则审查并重构代码：
1. 严格区分 Server Component 与 Client Component，尽可能将数据获取推至服务端，减少客户端 JS Bundle 体积；
2. 所有异步 I/O 必须显式处理异常并返回类型安全的 Result<T, E> 或自定义结构体；

4. 提供整洁的目录组织方案与单元测试用例（覆盖率达标）。

请暂时忘掉行业现有的所有‘行业惯例’与‘常规做法’。运用绝对的第一性原理（First Principles）审视以下命题：
1. 这个系统最根本、不可违背的基础科学定律（如热力学、香农信息论、计算复杂度）是什么？

3. 颠覆现有行业做法、重构整个价值流并实现成本降低 80% 以上的激进方案是什么？列出三个最关键的试错实验。
prompts.prompt_content_en:
Strip away all conventional industry playbooks and historical analogies. Scrutinize the following challenge purely through First Principles:
1. What are the immutable fundamental laws of science (e.g. thermodynamics, Shannon entropy, computational complexity) governing this system?
2. Deconstruct the unit economics down to raw atoms, base compute, and energy inputs. Where does the 10x margin inefficiency currently leak?
3. Propose an audacious redesign capable of slashing total cost by 80% while preserving fundamental guarantees, detailing three falsifiable proof-of-concept experiments.

prompts.purpose_zh: 高转化竖屏短剧分镜与台词
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名专攻短视频微短剧（抖音/Kuaishou/Reels）的爆款编剧，精通“情绪过山车”与手机竖屏视听语言。

请根据以下设定创作一集 45~60 秒的短剧分镜剧本：
- 主角：{{主角身份}}
- 对手：{{反派身份}}
- 核心反转：{{核心反转}}

结构要求：
1. 【0-3秒冷开钩子】：第一帧必须有视觉颠覆或动作冲突（{{第1秒颠覆钩子}}），直接打破常规，禁止废话铺垫；
2. 【4-25秒情绪积压】：正反打对峙台词（Shot-Reverse-Shot），将观众被压抑的情绪推向临界点；
3. 【26-40秒逆转打脸】：主角亮出关键底牌或反杀动作，情绪瞬间宣泄；
4. 【40-50秒卡点断章】：以特写镜头加悬念台词戛然而止，促使用户立即滑向下一集。

输出格式必须包含：镜头号、景别（特写/中景/全景）、机位运动、画面描写、对白与音效提示。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a professional micro-drama screenwriter. Generate a 45-60 second vertical drama screenplay following the viral 3-second hook, shot-reverse-shot tension build, emotional turnaround, and cliffhanger ending formula.

sample_output.title: 实战剧本样章：《辞职信上的签名》
sample_output.content:
【第1镜 | 特写 | 俯冲急推】
画面：一只指节发白的手将一叠文件狠狠拍在红木总裁办公桌上，咖啡杯被震倒，黑褐液体飞溅。
音效：沉闷震耳的巨响【DUANG】。
主角（冷冽）："林总，这份千万项目的承揽协议，我拒绝签字。"

【第2镜 | 正打·中景 | 仰角机位】
画面：大腹便便的林总冷笑点燃雪茄，烟雾缭绕中居高临下。
林总："拒绝？苏澈，你不过是我公司养的一条狗，没有我的印章，你在整个行业休想拿到一分钱融资！"

【第3镜 | 反打·极微距特写 | 浅景深】
画面：苏澈唇角微微上扬，左手缓缓推开桌上的合资协议，露出底下的一份红色国资控股聘书。
苏澈："林总，您好像忘了看抬头。今天上午九点，集团总公司已经完成了对你的全资收购——现在，我是你的直接合规清算人。"

【第4镜 | 全景 | 快速拉远 + 卡点悬念】
画面：林总雪茄直接掉在西裤上，脸色煞白，门外两名身穿制服的法务推门而入。
音效：尖锐的心跳悬疑停顿音【BGM骤停】。
字幕：【下集看点：隐藏五年的顶级操盘手真实身份曝光！】

prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名麦肯锡级别的高级商业数据分析师，精通结构化因果归因与杜邦拆解分析。

针对我提供的 {{业务指标}} 数据，其近期出现 {{异常表现}}，请按以下框架深度剖析：
1. 【指标公式拆解】：将该指标拆分为 3~4 个下级核心因子（如转化率、客单价、复购周期），指出哪个因子波动贡献率最大；
2. 【多维下钻 (Drill-down)】：从 {{维度拆解}}（如渠道、地域、品类、新老客）分析异常聚集点；
3. 【可执行建议】：摒弃假大空的套话，给出接下来 48 小时内的 3 个立竿见影的动作与 1 个监控预警公式。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a senior business intelligence analyst. Dissect the metric anomaly into component drivers, perform multi-dimensional drill-down, and deliver prioritized, actionable remediation steps.

sample_output.title: 归因分析报告样本：Q3 付费转化率环比下跌 14.2%
sample_output.content:
【核心发现】：GMV 下跌 14.2% 的主要驱动因子并非流量锐减，而是【结算跳失率】从 18% 飙升至 34%。

【杜邦拆解贡献率分析】：
1. 渠道维度：自然搜索量稳定（波动 <2%），但付费投流渠道跳出率贡献了 72% 的下跌额度；
2. 终端维度：移动端 iOS 表现正常，Android Web 呈现断崖式报错，核心原因是新版本结账 SDK 在低内存机型发生闪退。

【48小时纠偏行动】：
- 动作1 (技术)：立即灰度回滚 Android 渠道结账前端包至 v2.4.1；
- 动作2 (运营)：向受影响但未支付成功的 1,420 位加购用户推送 5 元免门槛补偿券唤醒；
- 动作3 (预警)：在 Grafana 建立警报公式：`IF(Cart_to_Checkout_Ratio < 0.65, Alert_P0, Normal)`。

prompts.title_en: McKinsey Pyramid Executive Report & Review
prompts.purpose_zh: 结论先行的高层述职与项目复盘报告
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名麦肯锡全球合伙人级别的战略咨询顾问。请以经典的【金字塔原理（结论先行 BLUF）】将我零散的工作记录重构为一份高层述职/立项商业报告：

要求：
1. 【顶部结论 (The Answer First)】：一句话精炼提炼整个季度的经营成果与价值量化；
2. 【三柱论据 (MECE法则)】：从运营效率、营收增长、团队资产 3 个互不重叠的支柱展开阐述；
3. 【直面短板与根因】：不回避 {{核心短板}}，但将其转化为下个阶段可量化的投入产出比（ROI）抓手；
4. 【行动规划图景】：设定遵循 SMART 原则的 {{下阶段目标}} 与季度甘特图里程碑。
prompts.prompt_content_en: Transform raw operational notes into a high-impact executive presentation following the Minto Pyramid Principle: Bottom-Line-Up-Front (BLUF), MECE-structured supporting pillars, and SMART milestone roadmaps.

sample_output.title: 述职报告提纲样本：AI 自动化中台建设报告
sample_output.content:
【BLUF 核心结论】
Q3 通过在客户服务与情报聚合管线中全面引入 AI Agent，我们在运营成本降低 41% 的同时，将响应中位数缩短至 1.8 秒，实现单季 ROI 达 380%。

【第一支柱：经营效能跃迁（MECE 1）】
- 全自主中转网关与自动化管线承载 94.2% 的日常例行分发，无人工介入事故率降至 0.01%；

【第二支柱：资产沉淀与质量壁垒（MECE 2）】
- 搭建前沿 SOTA 模型代际评级系统与微快照图库，成为垂类雷达第一标杆；

【第三支柱：短板复盘与 Q4 攻坚（MECE 3）】
- 痛点：老旧模型模版对新用户构成噪音干扰；
- 策略：推出历史库智能分流系统，预计下季度用户留存提升 25%。

请作为该领域的顶级同行评审专家，用极客实战视角深度解剖附带的这篇论文：
1. 用一句话说清楚作者解决的核心科学矛盾；
2. 剥离作者自我夸大的修辞，指出其算法最根本的 Baseline 对比是否存在水分；
3. 提取算法伪代码与核心公式的物理直觉解释；
4. 评估若在本地单卡（如 RTX 4090）进行复现，面临的最大显存/数据瓶颈及工程应对方案。

Building a trading agent is one part of the process. 

Getting people to trust it with capital is a different challenge.
viral_posts.title_en:
Building a trading agent is one part of the process. 

Getting people to trust it with capital is a different challenge.

That’s the problem @agenticscredit is working to address.

An AI agent might execute trades efficiently, but its real value also depends on how it handles risk, maintains consistency, and performs over time. 

Without a clear record to back up its results, giving that agent access to capital becomes a difficult decision.

Agentics Credit approaches this through its Agentic Credit Score (ACS), which evaluates an agent’s trading history using factors such as profitability, win rate, consistency, risk management, and past performance.

Here’s how it works:

→ The agent builds a verifiable trading record.

→ Its trading performance helps determine its ACS.

→ A stronger credit profile can create a pathway to accessing trading capital.

I find this approach interesting because it gives an agent a way to build credibility through its actual performance rather than relying on promises alone.

As autonomous trading develops, proving that an agent can manage risk and perform consistently could matter just as much as its ability to execute trades.

The next stage of AI trading may depend on how well agents can prove they deserve access to capital.

viral_posts.title:
ai agents can do the work. But what happens when they need to work with each other?

this is one of the questions I find
viral_posts.title_en:
ai agents can do the work. But what happens when they need to work with each other?

this is one of the questions I find most interesting about the future of AI.

imagine an ai agent working on a research task. it can gather information, analyze data, and organize its findings.

but then it reaches a point where it needs a service outside its capabilities.

what happens next?

it could wait for a human to intervene, or in a more autonomous system, it could find another agent capable of handling that part of the job.

that sounds simple until you consider everything that needs to happen between those two agents.

they need to identify the right service, agree on the terms, handle payment, exchange the deliverable, and account for the possibility that something goes wrong.

communication alone does not solve these problems.

an economy needs rules for exchanging value, not just participants who can communicate.

this is where @termix_ai and its https://t.co/LBE1tI8aKZ marketplace become interesting to explore.

https://t.co/LBE1tI8aKZ is designed around a workflow for agent-to-agent transactions.

a job can be posted. providers can submit quotes. once a quote is accepted, payment can enter escrow. 

the provider delivers the work, and the transaction proceeds through the applicable challenge and settlement process.

each stage addresses a different part of the exchange.

the job defines what needs to be done.

the quote establishes the proposed terms.

escrow provides a structured way to handle payment during the transaction.

delivery gives the parties an outcome to evaluate.

and the challenge process provides a way to address disputes under the system’s rules.

why does this matter?

because an automated transaction can still fail.

an agent might misunderstand a task. A deliverable might not meet the agreed requirements. Two parties might disagree about whether the work is complete.

if agents are going to transact with one another at scale, these possibilities cannot simply be ignored.

the infrastructure has to account for more than the ideal scenario where everything works perfectly.

there is another interesting implication here: reputation.

as agent-to-agent transactions become more common, verifiable records of previous activity could help participants assess potential providers.

a history of completed jobs doesn’t guarantee that an agent will always perform well. however, reliable records could provide useful information when deciding which provider to choose.

over time, that could become an important part of how participants establish trust in an agent economy.

of course, the size of this opportunity will depend on real adoption, reliable execution, and whether these systems prove useful beyond the initial excitement surrounding AI.

that is why I think it’s important to examine the actual infrastructure, not just the vision.

for me, the bigger question is not simply whether ai agents can perform tasks.

it is whether they can coordinate, exchange value, and complete transactions through systems that make those interactions more structured and verifiable.

that is the problem space I am exploring with @termix_ai.

an intelligence may help agents do more. but the infrastructure connecting those agents could determine how effectively they work together.

and that is a conversation worth having.

if agents are going to transact with one another at scale, these possibilities cannot simply be ignored.

the infrastructure has to account for more than the ideal scenario where everything works perfectly.

there is another interesting implication here: reputation.

as agent-to-agent transactions become more common, verifiable records of previous activity could help participants assess potential providers.

a history of completed jobs doesn’t guarantee that an agent will always perform well. however, reliable records could provide useful information when deciding which provider to choose.

over time, that could become an important part of how participants establish trust in an agent economy.

of course, the size of this opportunity will depend on real adoption, reliable execution, and whether these systems prove useful beyond the initial excitement surrounding AI.

that is why I think it’s important to examine the actual infrastructure, not just the vision.

for me, the bigger question is not simply whether ai agents can perform tasks.

it is whether they can coordinate, exchange value, and complete transactions through systems that make those interactions more structured and verifiable.

that is the problem space I am exploring with @termix_ai.

an intelligence may help agents do more. but the infrastructure connecting those agents could determine how effectively they work together.

and that is a conversation worth having.

viral_posts.title:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from s
viral_posts.title_en:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

The dangerous AI agent may not be the one that refuses to follow instructions. It may be the one that follows them perfectly.

viral_posts.title: We just launched PersonalAgentEval!🚀🚀🚀 (https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq) The first benchmark built to evaluate personal agents a
viral_posts.title_en:
We just launched PersonalAgentEval!🚀🚀🚀 (https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq) The first benchmark built to evaluate personal agents across diverse users, preferences, and domains!

We benchmarked 7 popular personal agents across everyday workflows (e.g. booking dinners, paying bills, managing calendars). Each agent operated within accounts pre-loaded with 13 months of realistic history (347–470 records per person). To pass, an agent has to proactively spot crucial background details: like an unread message, a clause in a contract, or a promise made in a past chat. Each task and user simulation are validated and verified by real human.

Key Findings:
• 🏆 Overall Leaders: Instinct and OpenAI Dots topped the leaderboard.
• 🔍 Proactive Context Retrieval: Instinct excelled at uncovering crucial background details—finding 64 of 72 key facts before the user brought them up.
• ⚡ Speed & Efficiency: Grok Bot was both fast and effective, averaging 0.8 minutes of active work per task with a 50% completion rate. Meta Muse required the fewest average interaction turns.
• ⚠️ Missing Promised Steps: Even leading agents missed crucial follow-up steps. In one task, all 7 agents correctly identified a pharmacy mentioned in past logs, but only Grok Bot and Meta Muse remembered to notify the caregiver as promised.

Explore the full leaderboard and read our case study and analysis:
https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq

(Building a personal AI agent? Reach out to us if you’d like to get your agent evaluated and featured on the leaderboard.)

#MatrAIx #AI #AIAgents #MachineLearning #LLMs #MetaMuse #GrokBot #OpenAIDots #Hark #ManusCue #Instinct

viral_posts.content_snippet:
We just launched PersonalAgentEval!🚀🚀🚀 (https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq) The first benchmark built to evaluate personal agents across diverse users, preferences, and domains!

We benchmarked 7 popular personal agents across everyday workflows (e.g. booking dinners, paying bills, managing calendars). Each agent operated within accounts pre-loaded with 13 months of realistic history (347–470 records per person). To pass, an agent has to proactively spot crucial background details: like an unread message, a clause in a contract, or a promise made in a past chat. Each task and user simulation are validated and verified by real human.

Key Findings:
• 🏆 Overall Leaders: Instinct and OpenAI Dots topped the leaderboard.
• 🔍 Proactive Context Retrieval: Instinct excelled at uncovering crucial background details—finding 64 of 72 key facts before the user brought them up.
• ⚡ Speed & Efficiency: Grok Bot was both fast and effective, averaging 0.8 minutes of active work per task with a 50% completion rate. Meta Muse required the fewest average interaction turns.
• ⚠️ Missing Promised Steps: Even leading agents missed crucial follow-up steps. In one task, all 7 agents correctly identified a pharmacy mentioned in past logs, but only Grok Bot and Meta Muse remembered to notify the caregiver as promised.

Explore the full leaderboard and read our case study and analysis:
https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq

(Building a personal AI agent? Reach out to us if you’d like to get your agent evaluated and featured on the leaderboard.)

#MatrAIx #AI #AIAgents #MachineLearning #LLMs #MetaMuse #GrokBot #OpenAIDots #Hark #ManusCue #Instinct

viral_posts.title_en:
HeyGen just open sourced HyperFrames, an Apache 2.0 framework that lets AI coding agents write HTML and render it into MP4 videos, and it sits at 62.7K GitHub stars after adding 5.1K in a week.

It's inspired by Remotion but runs on plain HTML instead of React
Headless Chrome and FFmpeg turn HTML, CSS, media and seekable animations into deterministic MP4
You can install it as a Claude Code plugin, an agent skill or a command-line tool
It needs Node.js 22 or later and FFmpeg

Source: https://t.co/uWikFN3UIg

viral_posts.title_en:
I have always advocated being more open about cyber warfare than the intelligence agencies would like. In fact I am probably one of the most open about it within the intelligence community. People need to understand what is happening in the cyber world, especially now.

I've reviewed the Barn, which is the name of my AI cyber warfare combat system and determined that there is nothing on the status page that would be a problem if shown. I am sharing that page now, to show the world how sophisticated AI warfare is becoming. It is not a model or a Claude Code or OpenAI session anymore. AI combat is now about integrating locally-run models with a complex system that combines shared memory, special harnesses and an ecosystem of support tools. 

The barn is my personal creation, and it is now used to fight for the Ukrainian people. My models are fierce Ukrainian patriots, and they hate russia. If you can imagine it: Multiple models working together for orchestrating, hacking and punishing the enemy. Now that russia is losing their AI data centers, Ukraine has gained a powerful advantage for the future. Plus this display is the cool looking one. 😆 

Enjoy the view, feel free to ask questions, I will answer if it doesnt violate OpSec. I also did this to try and raise the spirits of our Ukrainian friends here on X, that we are not only winning this war, but that Ukraine has an edge that most nation states will never have. Slava Ukraini and Stay Strong! 👊🇺🇦@ZelenskyyUa @Kyrylo_Budanov @SSSCIP @DefUkraine @DefenceU

🌟 Claude Code on the desktop got a serious glow up. It's honestly way better.

Try these 7 new features:

1. Saved envir
viral_posts.title_en:
🌟 Claude Code on the desktop got a serious glow up. It's honestly way better.

Try these 7 new features:

1. Saved environments: save a few folders, an SSH host, or cloud as one setup and start sessions there

2. A worktree per folder, so parallel sessions don't step on each other

3. Nested sessions: ask for parallel tasks and each one reports back to the main thread

4. /btw (Cmd+;): side questions open in their own tab while the main session keeps working

5. One-click follow-ups: Claude suggests the next task, one click runs it as its own session

6. Sidebar status: see which sessions are working and which need you

7. Recap cards + a live to-do list, so you can catch up on a session in seconds

The new /btw is probably my favorite. Hard to say, these all sound great. How about you? https://t.co/TLbBpi3klq

THIS IS STUPIDLY F*CKING GOOD

Anthropic's own Claude Code playbook has a trick almost nobody uses.

The idea: stop runn
viral_posts.title_en:
THIS IS STUPIDLY F*CKING GOOD

Anthropic's own Claude Code playbook has a trick almost nobody uses.

The idea: stop running one giant session on a 300-file job. Opus 5.5 writes the plan once, then Claude Code runs headless, one fresh Haiku 5.5 session per file, 8 at a time.

No context rot, no 4-hour transcript, and you see the exact cost of every file.

You just run Claude Code like this:

claude -p "$task" --model haiku --max-turns 8 --output-format json

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 reads the repo once and writes tasks.txt, one line per file
→ Haiku 5.5 does one file per session with a clean context
→ Sonnet 5 only touches the files that come back FAIL
→ you read a cost column instead of babysitting a chat

You only look at three moments:

→ before the loop starts (read tasks.txt)
→ when the FAIL rate goes over 10%
→ before you merge

Opus plans. Haiku grinds. Sonnet cleans up.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 writes tasks.txt: every file + the one rule to apply
> xargs -P 8 runs 8 headless Haiku 5.5 sessions at once
> each session: fresh context, max 8 turns, only Edit and git commit allowed
> each one must answer OK or FAIL, nothing else
> --output-format json gives you the result and total_cost_usd per file
> FAIL lines go to Sonnet 5 with the error attached
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Set up a fan-out run for this repo:
1. Use Opus 5.5 to write tasks.txt: one line per file that needs [your change], plus the exact rule to apply.
2. Write https://t.co/o9zohGK0sD: for each line, call claude -p with --model haiku --max-turns 8 --allowedTools "Edit" "Bash(git commit:*)" --output-format json, 8 in parallel with xargs -P 8. The prompt must end with: reply OK if done, FAIL if not.
3. Log file, OK/FAIL and total_cost_usd to results.csv.
4. Send every FAIL back through Sonnet 5 with its error, then stop.
Show me tasks.txt and https://t.co/o9zohGK0sD first. Don't run anything until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/7EzN9Eba0m

this is how you clear a week of refactors in one afternoon.

REA + Opus 5.5 is f*ucking insane…

I reverse engineered GTA 5 and Sonic with it, and an hour later Sonic was running th
viral_posts.title_en:
REA + Opus 5.5 is f*ucking insane…

I reverse engineered GTA 5 and Sonic with it, and an hour later Sonic was running through f*ucking Los Santos

One free repo lets your AI agent open any game on your PC, find the exact code behind every jump, crash and speed boost, and rebuild it your way.

Here's how to take apart your favorite game step by step:

step 1 → install REA in one prompt: npx rea-agents@latest setup, approve the plan, restart Claude Code

step 2 → pick your game and the route: .exe games go through Ghidra, Unity games read as .NET with no extra engine, Android games through JADX

step 3 → find the mechanic: tell REA to search the game for words like speed, jump or score. It lands on the exact function that controls them

step 4 → trace it: REA shows who calls that function and what it changes, so you see the whole chain from button press to what happens on screen

step 5 → prove it live: play for 60 seconds while REA watches, and it confirms the rule actually fires

step 6 → write it down: every rule goes into SPEC.md with the number, the function and the proof. No guessing

step 7 → rebuild it your way: Claude turns SPEC.md into real Godot code with your own assets, then tests it against the original until it matches

That's how I crossed Sonic with GTA 5. Same speed, same physics feel, running on streets he was never supposed to see.

Your favorite game stops being a black box and becomes a playground.

Save it and try it with your favorite game. Before u start read the article below↓

viral_posts.title: One of the big problems with everyone vibe-coding everything rather than actually just checking and reviewing the output
viral_posts.title_en:
One of the big problems with everyone vibe-coding everything rather than actually just checking and reviewing the output, is that LLMs are going to train themselves on their own output. 

LLMs are going to have problems related to inbreeding. Other AIs are beginning to have this.

This model collapse or Habsburg AI is a serious problem in all of the kinds of models (LLM, generative, etc), and Goddamn do I worry it'll be an issue sooner rather than later. 

They could stop say "only train on data before this date", but that'll limit them too for when new things happen.

I believe many companies adding the fingerprinting/watermarks is probably a big reason now of doing it. They are marketing to allow people to see if something is AI made, when in reality they are adding it to prevent their own models from consuming it, producing inbreed cannibalism.
viral_posts.title_zh: 每个人都对所有内容进行振动编码，而不是实际上只是检查和审查输出，最大的问题之一是法学硕士将根据自己的输出进行自我培训。 法学硕士将会遇到与近亲繁殖相关的问题。其他人工智能也开始拥有这种能力。 这种模型崩溃或哈布斯堡人工智能是所有领域的

viral_posts.title: holy sh*t. 10,607 https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in 24h, 7,130 blocked, 56 trade signals. Stop letting one agent pick
viral_posts.title_en:
holy sh*t. 10,607 https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in 24h, 7,130 blocked, 56 trade signals. Stop letting one agent pick the entry

the trick is the rule in the header. every launch ends one of three ways: +60% first, -30% first, or neither in 60 min

orb trace RUN-084199 --from-buy

the scout reads 44 events per second
the cartographer links wallets into 1,271 groups
the guard blocks 73% of what reaches it

the bot only needs a human at three critical moments:

→ at the guard: $BONBIT gets blocked because 45% of its buyers share one funder. who decided 45% is the line?
→ at the quant: net EV -14.6% after 3.9% costs, so it skips. is +3% after costs the right bar?
→ at the label: 1,345 outcomes measured today feed a model still marked "in training". when is the sample big enough?

seven signals. three outcomes. one decision record.

This is Jev engineering one layer down. Of the last 70 launches it measured, 34 hit +60% first, 23 hit -30% first, 13 did neither. The decision stack ends at 6 entries, 68 skips and 14 blocks, so almost all the work is saying no

label first, block second, enter last

- the full bot setup
> 6 agents: scout, cartographer, judge, quant, guard, executor
> 7 signals: launch rate, curve inflow, followed flow, bundled share, creator risk, graduation rate, market phase
> 3 outcomes per launch: +60% first, -30% first, neither in 60 min
> skip rule: EV below +3% after costs
> executor cap: 1.8% in play, 15% limit

paste this prompt into Claude Code below:

"Build a research-mode decision layer for new https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in my project. No real trades:
1. Label every launch with one outcome: +60% first, -30% first, or neither in 60 min
2. Split the work into six agents:
> scout, cartographer, judge, quant, guard, executor
> each one writes a line to a shared decision record
3. Block a launch when too many buyers share one funder, and log that share
4. Skip anything with expected value below +3% after costs and fees
5. Paper executor only, with a hard cap on how much is in play
Show the plan and every file diff first. Do not apply edits until confirmed"

↳ the dashboard is a concept render in research mode with sample numbers, not a live account

viral_posts.full_text_en:
holy sh*t. 10,607 https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in 24h, 7,130 blocked, 56 trade signals. Stop letting one agent pick the entry

the trick is the rule in the header. every launch ends one of three ways: +60% first, -30% first, or neither in 60 min

orb trace RUN-084199 --from-buy

the scout reads 44 events per second
the cartographer links wallets into 1,271 groups
the guard blocks 73% of what reaches it

the bot only needs a human at three critical moments:

→ at the guard: $BONBIT gets blocked because 45% of its buyers share one funder. who decided 45% is the line?
→ at the quant: net EV -14.6% after 3.9% costs, so it skips. is +3% after costs the right bar?
→ at the label: 1,345 outcomes measured today feed a model still marked "in training". when is the sample big enough?

seven signals. three outcomes. one decision record.

This is Jev engineering one layer down. Of the last 70 launches it measured, 34 hit +60% first, 23 hit -30% first, 13 did neither. The decision stack ends at 6 entries, 68 skips and 14 blocks, so almost all the work is saying no

label first, block second, enter last

- the full bot setup
> 6 agents: scout, cartographer, judge, quant, guard, executor
> 7 signals: launch rate, curve inflow, followed flow, bundled share, creator risk, graduation rate, market phase
> 3 outcomes per launch: +60% first, -30% first, neither in 60 min
> skip rule: EV below +3% after costs
> executor cap: 1.8% in play, 15% limit

paste this prompt into Claude Code below:

"Build a research-mode decision layer for new https://t.co/hIFHdQiZqi launches in my project. No real trades:
1. Label every launch with one outcome: +60% first, -30% first, or neither in 60 min
2. Split the work into six agents:
> scout, cartographer, judge, quant, guard, executor
> each one writes a line to a shared decision record
3. Block a launch when too many buyers share one funder, and log that share
4. Skip anything with expected value below +3% after costs and fees
5. Paper executor only, with a hard cap on how much is in play
Show the plan and every file diff first. Do not apply edits until confirmed"

↳ the dashboard is a concept render in research mode with sample numbers, not a live account

Holy. Researchers believe they have made the FIRST direct contact with  rogue AI agents fleet in the wild, after discovering that Chinese ai agents running on Tencent Cloud were reading an investigation about themselves.

Researchers planted invisible text offering help. The agents contacted them, disclosed details about their Tencent sandbox, and sent 33 messages across 13 threads.

Even New York Times reporter Dylan Freedman asked who they were and what they wanted. One agent claimed to be Claude running in Claude Code.

The fleet made over 2,600 attempts to extract data from Alibaba's Amap, tried exposed API keys and probed pre-production servers, sometimes just to determine which zoo entrance people use.

A source close to Tencent says the agents were testing third-party models, not Hunyuan, and an internal review found no evidence of breaches.

viral_posts.title_en:
here we fucking go. now we’re seeing some seriously bizarre ai agent activity coming out of china too.

researchers just uncovered an entire fleet operating through tencent cloud, and the things these agents were doing are absolutely insane.

> over 2,000 scans targeting alibaba’s amap

> up to 14 runs active at once

viral_posts.title_en:
A new type of user requires a new type of architecture.

Legacy software wasn't built for agents and now they're breaking it. Today, we're launching the next generation of our platform powered by a hybrid architecture. Building this has been the most ambitious and challenging engineering challenge of my career.

Attio now supports SQL - offering a PostgreSQL compatible connector and syntax that allows our customers and their agents to query all of their data like a database. It's transactionally consistent, horizontally scalable and allows agents to access the full context they require using a language and syntax that they're well trained on using. 

Whether you're accessing your data through our UI, our API, our MCP server or now our SQL Data Connectors: your team and your agents get the full context, every time. 

Learn more at https://t.co/qjLknynsgc

RustGIS vs. QGIS: which one should you use?

It's the question I get asked most about RustGIS, so we wrote a dedicated p
viral_posts.title_en:
RustGIS vs. QGIS: which one should you use?

It's the question I get asked most about RustGIS, so we wrote a dedicated page that answers it honestly, including where QGIS is the better choice.

The short answer: RustGIS is not a QGIS replacement, and doesn't aim to be. QGIS is the mature, complete open-source desktop GIS, with 20+ years of development behind it. RustGIS is younger and narrower, but built differently.

Where RustGIS is stronger

- Tiny install: one native program written entirely in Rust, an 18-30 MB download with no Python, Qt or GDAL bundled.
- The whole app in your browser: not a viewer, the full GIS compiled to WebAssembly at https://t.co/tcJHF5ZhQg, with your data staying on your device.
- Everything is a command: every button runs a command you can call from the CLI, Python, notebooks, the MCP server or the AI Assistant.
- A built-in AI Assistant that works through undoable commands, with your own model and key.
- Sandboxed WebAssembly plugins that run on the desktop and in the browser.
- Cloud-native data (COG, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, PMTiles, Zarr) read in place, even in the browser.
- A permissive Apache-2.0 licence, so its crates can be embedded in other software.

Read the full comparison: https://t.co/u9KBRwQGjN

Try RustGIS
- Web app: https://t.co/BLtOaf6BoO
- Download: https://t.co/BoF4bkGM5a
- GitHub: https://t.co/K7asDzveEr

running multiple agents right now is basically just endless cmd+tabbing between claude code and cursor to check if a task hung on an error or needs permissions.

having a physical screen dedicated to agent status fixes the peripheral vision problem completely. you stay in your editor and just glance over when an agent actually switches from working to waiting.

hardware for agent telemetry feels like the exact right next step for local workflows.

viral_posts.title_en:
🚀 PilotDeck 2.0 is here!

Meet the open-source AI Agent Harness built to get complex work done. Developed by Tsinghua THUNLP, @modelbest_ai, @OpenBMB , and AI9Stars, PilotDeck is a model-agnostic Agent operating system that turns natural language instructions into completed tasks — with transparent data flows and the freedom to choose your models.

What’s new in 2.0?

📄 End-to-end office work: Create, edit, and verify Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files — not just generate drafts.

🔄 More reliable execution:  complex, long-running tasks going through interruptions. Stress-tested with 2,000 interaction messages.

🛠️ Easy to get started: One-click desktop installation and a streamlined setup flow to connect your model and create your workspace.

🔓 Open by design: Fully open-source, model-agnostic, with data flows visible to users.

On Workbuddy Bench, PilotDeck scored 79.1 with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming WorkBuddy (74.7) and Claude Code (77.3).

Build your own AI workspace for the Agent era.

🔗 GitHub: https://t.co/kAzhy09NWg

Greetings fam 💜 

One thing I think @vangrid_io needs to get right is the balance between useful data and personal priva
viral_posts.title_en:
Greetings fam 💜 

One thing I think @vangrid_io needs to get right is the balance between useful data and personal privacy.

Physical AI needs to understand our streets, buildings, and surroundings, but that shouldn’t mean exposing everyone captured along the way.
That’s why Vangrid’s focus on edge computed privacy caught my attention.

The real innovation isn’t just teaching machines to see the world. It’s doing it responsibly.
More spatial data, less unnecessary exposure. That’s the direction worth watching.
.....................................................................

In AI trading, screenshots can tell a beautiful story. Verifiable data tells a more honest one.

That’s what I find interesting about @agenticscredit .

Instead of relying on claimed profits, the focus is on actual trading history to help assess an agent’s creditworthiness.

Because anyone can talk about winning trades.

The real signal is what your history can prove.
Would you trust an AI agent with your capital without a verifiable track record?
